headline: Stocks steadied Friday after Thursday's oil-driven rout, but Brent near $97 and the 10-year yield at a fresh 18-month high keep the macro overhang firmly in place heading into a FOMC week.
stance: Cautiously defensive. The US-Iran conflict has pushed crude oil and Treasury yields to multi-month highs, squeezing corporate margins and reviving inflation fears — exactly the wrong backdrop ahead of a Federal Reserve decision on July 29 where markets price a ~71% chance of no rate cut. Intel's blowout Q2 (revenue nearly doubled estimates) shows the AI capex cycle is intact, but Alphabet's AI-spending anxiety last week is a reminder that the market wants proof of returns, not just spending. The path of least resistance is sideways-to-lower until the Fed and oil give clearer signals.

news.head: Houthi tanker attacks spike oil
news.body: Yemen's Houthi militants attacked two Saudi Arabian tankers in the Red Sea last week, sending Brent crude briefly above $100 per barrel for the first time since late May and reviving Strait of Hormuz supply-disruption fears.

news.head: Trump threatens Iranian infrastructure
news.body: President Trump threatened strikes on Iranian infrastructure in response to the Houthi attacks, adding a fresh escalation layer to a conflict now in its twelfth consecutive night of US-Iran military exchanges.

news.head: Alphabet and Tesla disappoint; Intel stuns
news.body: Alphabet fell ~7% and Tesla ~14% on Thursday after their earnings fueled concern about AI spending payback; Intel offset the gloom Friday with its strongest revenue growth in 15 years — $16.13 billion versus the $14.42 billion consensus — and adjusted EPS of $0.42, double the estimate.

news.head: ECB holds at 2.25%
news.body: The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.25% as expected on Thursday, having raised rates in June for the first time since 2023 in response to war-driven inflation pressure across the eurozone.

news.head: FOMC decision due Wednesday Jul 29
news.body: The Federal Reserve announces its rate decision this Wednesday; markets currently price roughly a 71% probability of no change, with the war-driven inflation impulse making a cut politically and analytically difficult.

news.head: S&P 500 breadth narrowing
news.body: Only 63% of S&P 500 stocks trade above their 50-day moving average and 42.6% of Nasdaq 100 stocks do the same — a sign that the index-level recovery masks thin participation beneath the surface.

implications: Oil at geopolitical-premium levels (WTI prior cash close $90.47, Brent $98.38 — both at the 91st–94th percentile of the past three years) is a direct tax on consumers and a renewed inflation input that complicates the Fed's path.
The 10-year Treasury yield (prior cash close 4.69%, an 18-month high) is pressing real rates to 2.43% — a historically high hurdle for equities valued at a CAPE of 40.5.

The yield curve (2s10s at +36 bps) is modestly positive but still historically flat, meaning the bond market is not pricing a robust recovery — it is pricing persistent inflation with limited Fed relief.

Positioning: Speculators are heavily positioned long S&P 500 futures (85th percentile of 3 years) — a contrarian warning for the index. Conversely, Russell 2000 futures sit at a 3-year extended short (4th percentile) — a contrarian floor for small-caps. In rates, 3M SOFR specs are at a 3-year extended short — a contrarian-bullish lean for front-end bonds. In FX, Euro and British Pound specs are both at extended shorts (10th and 15th percentiles) — a contrarian floor for both currencies vs. the dollar. In commodities, Copper specs are at the 96th percentile (extended long — a contrarian warning) and Wheat specs at the 98th percentile (extended long — a contrarian warning); WTI specs are at the 13th percentile (extended short — a contrarian floor for crude despite the geopolitical bid).
The equity-credit correlation at 0.69 means stocks and credit spreads are moving together — when oil spikes and yields rise, both sell off simultaneously, reducing diversification.

The USD (DXY prior cash close 101.46) remains firm, capping gold's upside despite safe-haven demand; gold (prior cash close $4,055.70) is stuck in a two-sided trade where geopolitics lift it but rising real yields and a strong dollar limit the rally.

watch.head: FOMC — Wed Jul 29, 2pm ET
watch.body: The most important event of the week: any hint that the Fed is debating a hike rather than a cut would be a shock to equities and bonds; a plain hold with a hawkish statement is the base case.

watch.head: Oil — Hormuz and Red Sea headlines
watch.body: Brent crude near $97 (Fri Jul 25 cash close) is the market's live geopolitical gauge — a break above $100 on new escalation would hit bonds and equities simultaneously.

watch.head: Durable Goods — Mon Jul 27, 8:30am ET
watch.body: Preliminary June durable orders are the first hard data point of the week; a miss would add to growth worries already visible in the CFNAI 3-month average sitting just below zero.

watch.head: USD/JPY at extreme
watch.body: The yen (prior cash close 163.79 ¥/$) sits at the 99.9th percentile of its 3-year range — meaning the dollar is as historically expensive versus the yen as it has ever been in three years; Bank of Japan meeting next week raises intervention or policy-shift risk.

watch.head: Consumer Confidence — Tue Jul 28
watch.body: July consumer confidence lands the day before the Fed; a weak print alongside $90+ oil would harden the stagflation narrative.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: 10-year Treasury yield prior cash close 4.69% — an 18-month high — as the oil-driven inflation revival pushes bond investors to demand more compensation for holding long-dated debt.
2-year Treasury yield prior cash close 4.33%; the 2s10s spread is +36 basis points (bps) — the curve is gently positive but not signaling confident growth expectations.

Real rates (inflation-adjusted yield) at 2.43% — a level that historically acts as a meaningful drag on equity valuations and housing; the 10-year breakeven inflation expectation sits at 2.26%, implying markets see oil-driven inflation as partly temporary.

Term premium (extra yield investors demand to hold long bonds) at 77.9 bps — elevated, meaning the bond market is pricing genuine uncertainty about the inflation and fiscal outlook, not just Fed policy.

Financial conditions remain accommodative overall: the Chicago Fed ANFCI is -0.55 (below zero means easier than average) and the St. Louis FSI is -0.70 — so despite higher yields, credit and money markets are not yet flashing stress.
4-week moving average of jobless claims at 208,000 — low by historical standards, suggesting the labor market has not yet cracked despite the oil and rate headwinds.
sections.positioning: 3M SOFR speculators sit at the 4th percentile of 3-year positioning — an extended short, meaning speculators have almost no bullish bets left on short-end rates. That is a contrarian floor: if the Fed signals any dovish lean on Wednesday, a sharp rally in front-end bonds is possible as shorts scramble to cover.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: S&P 500 prior cash close 7,411.98; Nasdaq 100 prior cash close 24,975.82; Dow prior cash close 51,947.25 — all reflect Thursday Jul 24's close after the oil-and-earnings-driven selloff.
Friday Jul 25 saw a partial recovery: SPY ETF was up ~0.36% and QQQ up ~0.29% in Friday pre-market, with oil pulling back ~2-3% from Thursday's spike providing relief.
VIX prior cash close 18.58 — elevated but not panicked; the SKEW index at 147.3 shows options traders are still paying a premium to hedge against a sharp downside move.
Breadth is thin: only 63.4% of S&P 500 stocks trade above their 50-day moving average, and just 42.6% of Nasdaq 100 stocks do — the rally has been narrow and top-heavy.
CAPE ratio at 40.5 and a negative equity risk premium (-2%) mean investors are paying peak prices for earnings while Treasuries now offer a real alternative — valuation provides no margin of safety.

Intel's Q2 blowout (revenue $16.13B vs $14.42B estimate, EPS $0.42 vs $0.21 estimate) is a bright spot for the semiconductor complex after the Philadelphia Semi Index entered a bear market earlier this month.
sections.positioning: S&P 500 futures speculators are at the 85th percentile of 3-year positioning — an extended long, meaning speculators are heavily positioned long — a contrarian warning. Russell 2000 futures are the mirror image: speculators are at the 4th percentile (extended short — a contrarian floor for small-caps). VIX futures specs are also at a 3-year extended short (10th percentile), which historically coincides with higher realized volatility ahead.

single_name.note: Jefferies Financial Group (broker-dealer) — company insiders have been buying, the stock trades above its 200-day moving average, dark-pool and options activity is live, and shorts are light (1.2 days to cover — minimal squeeze risk). A two-day consecutive signal makes this the highest-conviction long setup in this scan.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: High-yield credit spread over investment-grade at 277 bps — not distressed but wide enough to reflect genuine risk-off in the lower-quality end of the bond market.
Investment-grade option-adjusted spread at 79 bps — tight, suggesting large-cap corporate borrowers are not under funding stress.
FRA-OIS and SOFR-OIS both at 1 bp — the interbank funding market is essentially stress-free; there is no 2008-style plumbing risk in sight.
Commercial paper spread (CPFF) at 18 bps — short-term corporate funding remains orderly.
Bank credit growth at 6.4% year-over-year (as of mid-July) — healthy loan demand; the Fed's balance sheet is growing just 1.35% YoY, meaning bank lending, not Fed printing, is driving credit.

Overnight Reverse Repo (RRP) at just $0.7 billion — essentially zero — meaning excess cash has fully drained from money markets; bank reserves of $3,062 billion remain ample, but the liquidity buffer the system enjoyed in 2022-2024 is gone.

Treasury General Account (TGA) at $829.6 billion — a large government cash buffer that, if drawn down ahead of the debt ceiling, would inject reserves into the system and act as a modest liquidity tailwind.
